originalTitle: What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
summary: As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI's potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what's already happening. content: As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI’s potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what’s already happening. The Verge reached out to Disney, Netflix, Amazon, Lionsgate, and other studios who have started using AI, as well film startups focused on bringing generative AI into the mainstream to ask for their reaction to the recent warnings surrounding the technology. None have responded to our request for comment. The Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) and Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) did, however. The AI tools used in entertainment production differ from the AI systems that have sparked a recent round of whistleblowing and apocalyptic declarations. They do not seem to be as existentially dangerous as the AI systems that drove former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to quit his job and prompted Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger to insist that the technology could “kill all humans” at some point “within the next decade.”  But despite the differences between entertainment-focused AI and the models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, AI models that generate digital facsimiles of actors and attempt to replicate traditional filmmaking tools pose a threat to some human jobs. Similar to the way that the Hollywood unions advocated for protections and increased oversight around AI’s use during the 2023 strikes, Coxon’s Anthropic exit has inspired a wave of AI researchers to speak out in favor of stronger safety protocols. The heads of major AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and X have also called for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. While president Donald Trump has dismissed these concerns as overreactions, some other US politicians have felt pressured to take legislative action. Hollywood unions’ fight for strict rules around gen AI’s use did not stop the entertainment industry from embracing AI, but they have given Hollywood’s laborers a way to fight back in instances when they feel that AI tools are being used to harm them.  When I recently spoke with the Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists’ (SAG-AFTRA) chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree Ireland, he told me that the union recognized early on how AI could impact its members’ livelihoods. Most people might not have been familiar with the idea of studios completely replacing human actors with digital replicas, but SAG-AFTRA understood that it had an opportunity to shape public opinion about AI in Hollywood by “speaking out about it at the earliest possible point we could.”  “We bargained for and achieved enforceable, meaningful guardrails around how this technology can be implemented by the major employers in our industry,” Crabtree-Ireland explained. “That doesn’t include companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google directly, but it does encompass all of the companies who have built up businesses around the creation of professional level entertainment content in the United States.” Though Crabtree-Ireland believes we “should be concerned about the broader societal and social implications of AI,” he also thinks that some of the warnings about the technology being an extinction-level threat could potentially be hyperbole and overblown. Doomerism has become one of the more common ways that AI companies generate buzz around their products, but the fact that Coxon left Anthropic to sound the alarm has given Crabtree-Ireland pause. Hearing the message from “the CEOs of these companies or the billionaires who’ve made their billions off of doing the exact thing that they’re now warning us might not be good,” has left him unsure “what to trust or what to believe.” But he acknowledged that Coxon was able to achieve “traction with the public.” Getting people to believe that SAG-AFTRA’s fears about AI should be taken seriously was one of the union’s major goals when its members voted to strike. The key to doing that, Crabtree-Ireland told me, was leading the strike with a focused message that clearly laid out to the public what was at stake and steps that could be taken to prevent worst case scenarios. If not for that, Crabtree-Ireland thinks that the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) might not have agreed to some of the union’s demands like requiring that studios gain permission and compensate actors for the use of their AI-generated replicas. “If that principle hadn’t been established, I think the economic incentive to use replication and to replace human performances would have been much stronger” and “would have resulted in a much greater and faster adoption of digital replication.” Had the protections not been codified, Crabtree-Ireland is confident that entertainment workers would be in a much more dire position now. Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) executive director Sam Wheeler was much more pointed in his condemnation of the “tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society” whose recklessness “has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.” But while Wheeler finds it hard to take AI companies’ warnings at face value, he noted that the WGAE “has long warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to workers, to our democracy, and to the world.” “Guild members have bargained meaningful AI protections into their contracts; in 2023 WGA members spent 148 days on strike before the film and television studios agreed to real safeguards for film and television writers,” Wheeler said. “But collective bargaining is not a replacement for government regulation, and we are grateful to states like New York that continue to enact meaningful regulations in the absence of federal action.” Wheeler listed the disempowerment of workers, the degradation of the internet, the spread of disinformation, and increasing energy costs as some of the tangible societal harms AI has exacerbated. chineseTitle: 好莱坞对存在主义 AI 警告的看法
chineseSummary: 随着科技行业对人工智能毁灭人类的潜力发出警报，娱乐劳工组织敦促公众继续关注已经发生的事情。 The Verge 联系了迪士尼、Netflix、亚马逊、狮门影业和其他已经开始使用人工智能的工作室，以及专注于将生成式人工智能带入主流的电影初创公司 […]
chineseContent: 随着科技行业对人工智能毁灭人类的潜力发出警报，娱乐劳工组织敦促公众继续关注已经发生的事情。 The Verge 联系了迪士尼、Netflix、亚马逊、狮门影业和其他已经开始使用人工智能的电影公司，以及致力于将生成式人工智能带入主流的电影初创公司，询问他们对最近围绕该技术的警告有何反应。没有人回应我们的置评请求。然而，美国演员工会 - 美国电视和广播艺术家联合会 (SAG-AFTRA) 和美国东部作家协会 (WGAE) 却这样做了。娱乐制作中使用的人工智能工具与最近引发一轮举报和世界末日宣言的人工智能系统不同。它们似乎并不像人工智能系统那么危险，人工智能系统促使前人类研究员雅各布·考克森(Jacob Coxon)辞职，并促使人类联盟负责人埃文·哈宾格(Evan Hubinger)坚持认为，这项技术可能会在“未来十年内”的某个时刻“杀死所有人类”。  但是，尽管以娱乐为中心的人工智能与 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 开发的模型之间存在差异，但生成演员数字复制品并试图复制传统电影制作工具的人工智能模型对一些人类工作构成了威胁。与好莱坞工会在 2023 年罢工期间主张对人工智能的使用进行保护和加强监督的方式类似，Coxon 的 Anthropic 退出激发了一波人工智能研究人员公开支持更强有力的安全协议。 Anthropic、OpenAI、Google DeepMind 和 X 等主要人工智能公司的负责人也呼吁全行业放缓该技术的发展。尽管唐纳德·特朗普总统认为这些担忧是反应过度
